My dear [Augusta](/person/1180)
It is rather funny that the same post as brought your letter about [Lady Blachford’](/person/1253)s indignation brought one from an American Correspondent of [Gertrude](/person/1462)’s saying that she had observed that strict older sisters did generally turn out indulgent Mothers.[^1] But I understand it this way.

Wilmet had seen that strict laws had not fully answered with Fulbert, Angela or Bernard and the Harewoods were easygoing by nature and also there was a spirit of teasing in the family.

Bill’s goodness came from his friendship with Lance and I do not think indeed I said that outsides in the Navy or Army would have reported ill of the sons, they would do their work there properly, but they did love teasing – up to tyranny pitch as with Gerald when a small child
[the rest not reproduced]


[^1]: Wilmet Underwood, who in the early part of [The Pillars of the House](/book/109) is a strict but fair mother to her younger brothers and sisters, turns in the second part and in sequels into an indulgent parent whose unruly sons bully their cousins.
